power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: However, the global MITS evidence base is still dominated by facility-based MITS and child mortality surveillance.
Far less is known about conducting community-based MITS in rural settings across all age-groups, where logistical, operational, and social constraints differ markedly [18].

text.text: In addition to the time constraints in which to conduct MITS after death, community-based deaths pose unique challenges, including rapid burial expectations driven by cultural and religious practices, geographically dispersed families, delayed death notification to the study team, multigenerational decision-making involving elders, and mistrust or uncertainty about post-mortem procedures [19].

text.text: We address this gap through a structured process evaluation of the Vukamberi MITS project ("to examine" in Xitsonga).

We report key process and implementation outcomes (reach, adoption, fidelity, feasibility, acceptability and timeliness), the operational and sociocultural barriers encountered, and the adaptive strategies used to address them, and early operational and laboratory findings, to inform scalable approaches to community mortality surveillance.

We conducted a systematic process evaluation of the Vukamberi MITS Project, measuring implementation outcomes including notification timelines, consent rates, procedural completion, and sample adequacy, on all deaths recruited from 07 July 2024 to 30 June 2026.

The Vukamberi MITS protocol is the intervention being evaluated and is summarised narratively below, while the Agincourt HDSS is the platform within which the intervention was delivered and is summarised in the following section, with a full description in S1 Appendix.
The study protocol has not been published and is available from the corresponding author on request.

The Vukamberi MITS project is implemented in the Agincourt Health and Demographic Surveillance System (HDSS), though recruitment extended beyond the boundaries of the HDSS into the wider Bushbuckridge sub-district in Mpumalanga province, north-east South Africa.

text.text: Field staff screen every notified death against the eligibility criteria.

For eligible deaths, one male and one female communityfacing field worker jointly approach the family, in Xitsonga, Sepulana (Northern Sotho) or English, to obtain written informed consent, either at the household or, where household access is restricted or preferred by the family, at the mortuary; elder household members are engaged as consent mediators where appropriate.

Consented cases are sampled by a trained MITS team using standardised percutaneous needle biopsy of brain, lungs and liver, and of kidneys where field time allows (attempted for all cases rather than selected by cause of death, given its relevance to the post-mortem kidney sub-study), together with cerebrospinal fluid, blood and nasopharyngeal swabs, following MITS Surveillance Alliance standard operating procedures, with point-of-care serological testing performed at the time of sampling.
Specimens are transported to the in-house Agincourt laboratory for microbiology, with histopathology referred externally.
Results are combined with verbal autopsy and, where available, ante-mortem clinical records at a multi-disciplinary Determination of Cause of Death (DeCoDe) panel.
The cause of death is then returned in person to the family.

text.text: The Vukamberi project was assessed using a process evaluation framework integrating the Medical Research Council (MRC) Framework for Developing and Evaluating Complex Interventions [26], with Proctor's Implementation Outcomes Framework [27].

text.text: The MRC framework guided assessment of the intervention context, implementation mechanisms, and pathways through which inputs (community engagement, mortuary partnerships, trained field teams, laboratory capacity) enabled delivery of the community-based MITS workflow.
Seven implementation outcome domains were specified for this evaluation.
Four are Proctor constructs (adoption, fidelity, feasibility and acceptability).
Reach, timeliness and adaptations were added from complementary sources to capture features specific to community-based post-mortem surveillance.

Reach was taken from the RE-AIM framework [28] and corresponds to Proctor's penetration construct; timeliness is a core attribute in the CDC guidelines for evaluating public health surveillance systems [29] and was included because MITS must be performed soon after death, before decomposition compromises sample quality; and adaptations were documented as recommended by the MRC framework, which treats adaptation to context as central to complex intervention delivery [26].

text.text: The seven domains were operationalised as follows: reach (timely death notification and eligibility screening), adoption (family consent and enrolment), fidelity (adherence to MITS standard operating procedures), feasibility (procedural completion and sample adequacy), acceptability (cultural appropriateness of the process, including elder involvement in consent), timeliness (intervals from death to notification and sampling), and adaptations (modifications introduced in response to operational and sociocultural barriers).
This integrated approach enabled assessment of whether community-based MITS was feasible and of how specific mechanisms and contextual factors shaped implementation outcomes across phases (Fig 3).

text.text: Enrolment trajectories were analysed monthly to characterise programme rampup and phase-specific performance.

Implementation challenges and adaptive strategies were categorised as operational, logistical, sociocultural, or project-level, and mapped against the implementation domains and the phase in which they occurred, enabling a temporal analysis of barrier-adaptation relationships.

To describe change in implementation performance over time, the reach, adoption and feasibility indicators were additionally disaggregated by implementation year (Year 1: July 2024-June 2025; Year 2: July 2025-June 2026), and the enrolment cascade was tabulated cumulatively by quarter.
The protocol was open to decedents of all ages from inception, and the age distribution of the enrolled series was described to establish whether reach extended across age groups.
Age groups followed the study protocol: stillbirth, neonate (under 28 days), infant (28 days to under 1 year), child (1-16 years) and adult (older than 16 years).
Ethical approval was obtained from the University of the Witwatersrand Human Research Ethics Committee (M230754 MED23-07-051).
The study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and the Protection of Personal Information Act 4 of 2013 (POPIA).
Written informed consent was obtained from the next of kin of each enrolled decedent prior to any study procedures whom aged 18 years and above.
Participation was voluntary, and emotional and psychological support was offered to all bereaved families during and after the consent process.
Implementation proceeded through four phases: a preparatory phase before enrolment began, followed by a pilot, scale-up, and full surveillance across the 24-month period.
The preparatory phase (May-December 2023) established community and stakeholder engagement, formative acceptability work and ethics approval.
The pilot phase (July-December 2024) tested the standard operating procedures, established the community informant network and introduced mortuary-based consenting.
Scale-up (January-December 2025) extended the catchment area beyond the HDSS, incentivised community informants and formalised mortuary partnership agreements.

And finally, the full surveillance phase (January-June 2026) established the in-house culture bench, initiated the verbal autopsy and DeCoDe workflows, expanded the field team from one to two community liaison officers with an additional MITS assistant, and introduced buffer stock protocols following the kit supply gap.

Screening coverage was completed every month, while enrolment rose from fewer than five procedures per month in the pilot to 12-26 per month from June to November 2025 and, after a commodity stockout in early 2026, 14-15 per month from April to June 2026.

text.text: The enrolled series comprised 197 adults (95.6%) and 9 paediatric cases (4.4%, aged 4-16 years); two cases had incomplete age documentation but were confirmed as adults on secondary review.
No stillbirths, neonatal deaths, or infant deaths were enrolled during the study period.
The protocol was open to all ages from inception; the first paediatric case was enrolled in February 2025.
Infant deaths did occur in the catchment: two eligible infant deaths were notified but could not proceed because the families planned burial at sunset on the day of death (Table 5).

text.text: The absence of infant enrolments therefore points to lower community acceptability of MITS for infant deaths and to same-day burial practice for infants.
Elder household members were involved in consent discussions in 277/316 (87.7%) of eligible cases.
Elder involvement was associated with improved family receptiveness in field notes where initial hesitancy or intra-family disagreement had been documented.

text.text: Family refusal (53 cases, 48.2% of non-enrolled eligible cases) was the single largest reason for non-enrolment, documented in 18 of the 24 months of the study.
Reasons for refusal were recorded at monthly-summary level without the age or sex of the decedent, so variation in refusal by age or sex could not be assessed.
Refusals were heterogeneous (
Table 5): the most common driver was grief-related unreadiness, where families in the acute aftermath of bereavement were not yet able to engage with the consent process.
Traditional beliefs about bodily integrity and disturbance of the spirit of the deceased were documented in a subset of cases.

In several instances, families expressed fatalistic acceptance of the death particularly for elderly decedents as in one field-documented case where the family stated the deceased "was old, they had accepted the outcome and did not want her to be part of research."
In two cases, families explicitly declined further contact.

Monthly refusal rates were highest during 336 the early scale-up period (January-March 2025: 5 per month) and, apart from a return to five 337 in June 2025 (the peak enrolment month), remained at four or fewer per month thereafter as 338 community familiarity grew.
The monthly refusal trend is overlaid on Fig 5.

The concentration 339 of refusals in the months immediately following the extension of enrolment into newly engaged 340 villages suggests that community sensitisation should be completed before enrolment begins 341 in a new area.

text.text: All enrolled participants had tissue and, where obtainable, fluid samples successfully collected in accordance with the MITS standard operating procedures.
Specimen collection was nearcomplete for the principal diagnostic compartments.

Among the 206 enrolled cases, formalinfixed tissue was obtained from the brain in 203 (98.5%), right lung in 205 (99.5%), left lung 204 (99.0%) and the liver in 204 (99.0%); the four core solid organs were jointly sampled in 201 cases (97.6%).

Kidney tissue was obtained in a minority of cases (left 29 [14.1%], right 24 [11.7%]); kidney biopsy was attempted for all cases but was frequently constrained by available field time relative to the core diagnostic organs.

For microbiology, EDTA whole blood was collected in 203 cases (98.5%), blood culture bottles (aerobic and anaerobic) in 201 cases (97.6%), nasopharyngeal swabs in 205 (99.5%; collected but not yet tested, owing to cost constraints), and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) in 180 (87.4%), with paired solid-organ microbiology specimens obtained in 200 cases (97.1%).
Rectal swabs were not collected.

The study team decided against them when developing the protocol because the budget could not cover the multiplex molecular testing needed to distinguish enteric pathogens that contributed to death from normal gut flora.
Sample adequacy for the core specimen set was therefore high.
The collected specimens are distinct from completed analyses with laboratory processing, verbal autopsies, medical records linkage and determination of cause of death (DeCoDe) processes continuing.
As of June 2026, microbiological processing on the in-house culture bench had been finalised for 108 of 206 cases (52.4%).
The outstanding cases reflect laboratory throughput at the reporting cut-off, and processing was continuing at the close of the study period.

Drawing the domains together, implementation across the four phases was shaped by a recurring set of challenges: notification arriving more than 48 hours after death, emotional sensitivity in acutely bereaved families, cultural hesitancy about disfigurement and disturbance of the spirit of the deceased, mortuary-level access barriers, a traditional leader's restriction on entry to 14 villages, laboratory turnaround delays, and the MITS kit supply gap of January to mid-March 2026.

Each was met with an adaptation introduced at an identifiable point in the study and traceable to a change in the implementation outcomes reported above: the incentivised multi-channel notification network restored reach and reduced out-of-window notification; elder mediation and transparent non-disfigurement messaging raised consent; formal mortuary agreements and mortuary-based consenting preserved reach and procedural completion where household access failed; and the in-house culture bench shortened laboratory turnaround.

Taken together these adaptations describe an implementation model in which community-based MITS is sustained by the notification, consent and laboratory systems built around the sampling procedure (Table 6).

Adaptive strategies and associated outcomes reflect documented field team responses.
This study presents, to our knowledge, one of the first systematic process evaluations of establishing community-based all-ages MITS surveillance across all ages.

Over 24 months of enrolment, all 408 notified community deaths were screened, a MITS procedure was completed in all 206 consented cases with target-organ sampling adherence of 96.6%, and 65.2% of eligible families consented, indicating that community-based MITS is operationally feasible within an established rural surveillance platform.

Enrolment increased from fewer than five procedures per month in the pilot phase to 12-26 per month from June to November 2025 and recovered to 14-15 per month from April 2026 after the kit supply gap, consistent with iterative adaptation to context-specific barriers within the HDSS infrastructure [24, 26, 27].

text.text: The evaluation also extends the MITS evidence base: CHAMPS and most published MITS programmes have focused on stillbirths and child deaths, whereas Vukamberi applied the procedure to community deaths at all ages, including adults.

The diagnostic validity of MITS against complete diagnostic autopsy was established in hospital deaths in Mozambique, with cause-of-death concordance of 75.9% in adults, 89% in children, 83% in stillbirths, 68% in neonates and 68% in maternal deaths [30] [31] [32] [33]; whether that performance holds for community deaths sampled a median of 37 hours, and up to 72 hours, after death will be addressed by the Vukamberi cause-of-death analysis.

text.text: Screening of all notified deaths was maintained throughout the study, although this measures coverage of notified deaths rather than of all deaths in the catchment (see Limitations).
CHAMPS and comparable programmes typically target notification within 24-72 hours for paediatric deaths in both communities and health facilities [16].

text.text: Our 48-hour window for allage community deaths was chosen because high ambient temperatures in the study area accelerate body decomposition and bacterial overgrowth, and because of the culturally grounded practice among elders of waiting two to six hours after apparent death before calling the mortuary, which is linked to beliefs of possible 'miraculous recovery' [24, 34].

text.text: Only 26 deaths (6.4%) were ineligible because of delayed notification, a pattern consistent with community-based MITS programmes in other rural settings, including India and Pakistan, where cultural practices around death disclosure, geographic isolation and limited informant awareness contribute to delayed reporting [19, 20].

text.text: The multi-channel notification network, particularly incentivised community and mortuary informants, was the main strategy that sustained screening and reduced out-of-window notifications across study phases.

The 65.2% consent rate among eligible cases is lower than the 82% consent reported for paediatric deaths in a Mozambican hospital setting [17] but was achieved for community deaths of all ages within a 48-hour window and is consistent with the high hypothetical acceptability of MITS reported in this community during the Vukamberi formative study [24].

text.text: The dominant driver of non-enrolment was family refusal (48.2% of non-enrolled eligible cases), most often reflecting grief-related unreadiness.
This pattern aligns with evidence from consent research in acute bereavement contexts, which identifies emotional state at the time.

text.text: Most refusals reflected a mismatch between the 48-hour operational window and a family's capacity to engage in the consent process, and few families expressed principled opposition to MITS.

This has implications for programme design: advance community sensitisation that allows households to indicate openness to participation before bereavement, and flexible return-visit protocols, may increase enrolment without compromising consent.

The decline in refusals as community familiarity grew across phases supports this interpretation, although refusal reasons were recorded at summary level and could not be linked to decedent characteristics.
A distinctive feature of Vukamberi implementation was the strategic use of elder household members as consent mediators.

Our earlier qualitative study in this community documented how elder authority in Xitsonga-and Sepulana (Northern Sotho)-speaking communities in rural Mpumalanga is deeply embedded in death ritual governance; elders hold decision-making power over whether the deceased's body may be examined, and their endorsement is both socially required and practically decisive for family consent decisions [34].

text.text: This authority is not static: the same study found that younger household members increasingly defer to elders on decisions made around the time of death, such as whether the body may be examined, even in households where elders have less say in everyday matters.
Elder involvement was documented in 277/316 (87.7%) of eligible cases and was consistently associated with improved family receptiveness in field notes where initial hesitancy was documented.

This finding is consistent with evidence from the CHAMPS PICK-CHAMP participatory communityentry workshops, in which participants across five sites indicated that support for MITS was contingent on the procedure not interfering with burial practices and rituals, and in which engagement with community leaders was central to establishing acceptability [37].

A comparable emphasis on rapid identification of deaths and on prior institutional relationship-building was reported from Zambezia Province, central Mozambique, where these were identified as preconditions for timely sampling [35].

text.text: Target-organ sampling adherence of 96.6% (199/206 consented cases) indicates high procedural fidelity, supported by established mortuary partnerships and consistent team training.

The 48-hour eligibility window was set on operational grounds, reflecting ambient temperature, the absence of refrigeration in most households and local burial practice, rather than on a published post-mortem interval threshold.
The most significant operational disruption was the MITS kit supply gap from January to mid-March 2026, which resulted in 25 missed eligible cases at a time when families were willing to consent.

Cost-evaluation work in LMICs has identified MITS kits and consumables, alongside labour and testing, as principal cost drivers [38]; our experience shows that they are also a key operational vulnerability and underscores the need for buffer stock and procurement redundancy as projects move from externally funded pilots to integrated surveillance systems.

text.text: Because the scientific value of surveillance depends on population-representative sampling, such gaps introduce nonrandom missingness: a seasonal block of community deaths is absent from the series for reasons unrelated to the characteristics of those deaths.
Point-of-care (POC) testing was performed at the time of MITS sampling in 205 of 206 cases (99.5%).

Integrating POC testing for HIV, hepatitis B surface antigen, hepatitis C antibody and syphilis (RPR/TPHA) into the MITS procedure adds minimal procedural time and provides immediate serological context directly relevant to interpreting cause-of-death pathways, which may be useful for sites without rapid access to laboratory serology.

Viewed through an implementation science lens, the Vukamberi trajectory illustrates core principles of effective complex intervention implementation: staged rollout with deliberate preparatory investment prior to procedures; iterative adaptation in response to identified barriers; and system-level capacity building, including in-house culture bench establishment and mortuary partnership formalisation that improved project performance over time [26].

text.text: The preparatory phase (May-December 2023), focused on community engagement, stakeholder mapping, and formative acceptability work, was important for building the social licence necessary to conduct post-mortem procedures in bereaved households in a context where mistrust of biomedical research remains a real concern.

Our Phase 1 qualitative study reported that MITS was broadly acceptable in this community, with community members expressing willingness to participate provided the procedure was non-disfiguring, respectfully conducted, and that results would be shared back with families and the community; concerns about spirit disturbance and organ harvesting were raised and were specifically addressed through the pictorial consent aids and community information sessions developed as part of that preparatory phase [24].

text.text: This study has several strengths.

First, the evaluation integrated MRC process evaluation guidance with Proctor's Implementation Outcomes Framework, allowing implementation outcomes to be linked to specific mechanisms and contextual factors; to our knowledge, it is . among the first systematic process evaluations of community-based MITS and the first to cover deaths at all ages within an HDSS.

Second, implementation outcomes were derived from records generated prospectively as the intervention ran (notification logs, consent documentation, field and case reports and laboratory quality records) rather than reconstructed retrospectively, so barriers and the adaptations made in response are dated and can be read against the performance indicators of the period in which they occurred.
Third, reporting follows the Standards for Reporting Implementation Studies (StaRI) statement (S1 Checklist) [40].
text.formatted: Third, reporting follows the Standards for Reporting Implementation Studies (StaRI) statement (S1 Checklist) <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">[40]</ref>.

text.text: This evaluation also has limitations.

First, implementation outcomes were abstracted from monthly summary reports rather than case-level records, so reasons were not documented for 23 ineligible and 3 non-enrolled cases, and refusals could not be stratified by decedent age, sex or duration of terminal illness; these should be captured routinely in future surveillance.

Second, study notifications were not compared with deaths recorded independently by the HDSS, so the completeness of death ascertainment, overall and by age group (including infant deaths), could not be quantified; screening coverage refers to notified deaths only, and ascertainment was incomplete in February 2026, when only two mortuaries reported.

Third, the traditional leader's restriction of access to 14 villages and the kit supply gap of early 2026 may have introduced selection bias into the enrolled series, which may affect the representativeness of future cause-of-death estimates.
Fourth, the enrolled series was predominantly adult and included no stillbirths, neonates or infants, so feasibility for these groups could not be assessed.
Fifth, cause-of-death determination was incomplete at the reporting cut-off, so the diagnostic yield of community-based MITS is not reported here.

Sixth, the evaluation was conducted by the implementing team, which may have influenced the interpretation of field notes; the use of prospectively recorded operational data reduces, but does not remove, this risk.
Finally, the single-site design limits generalisability, although the Agincourt setting shares structural features with many surveillance sites in sub-Saharan.
Africa, including rural geography, high HIV burden, incomplete civil registration and strong community leadership.

The Vukamberi project demonstrates that community-based MITS surveillance is feasible, operationally achievable, and generates actionable scientific data within an established HDSS in rural South Africa.

Elder-mediated consent, mortuary partnerships, multi-channel incentivised death notification and in-house laboratory capacity may be transferable to sites facing comparable barriers in the African region, and reliable procurement of consumables is a precondition for continuous surveillance.

Africa CDC's Continental Framework for Mortality Surveillance calls for community mortality surveillance to be integrated into national health information systems [39]; the Vukamberi experience illustrates what such integration requires in practice.
